summary: Trust Layer is an offline layer that re-checks an alarm already raised by a crew health monitor. On a Mars mission, ground support can be up to about 24 minutes away, and hospital studies show most monitor alarms are false. When the monitor raises an alarm, Trust Layer takes the last 10 seconds of ECG and pulse (PPG), gives a score, and shows a verdict with one reason. The original alarm is never hidden. On 482 ICU alarms the model had never seen, 92% of its red alarms were real, against 28% if every alarm is trusted. It runs in about 30 ms on a laptop with no cloud. Limits: Earth ICU data, not astronauts; ventricular tachycardia alarms only; not for clinical use.
details:
WHAT IT DOES. An existing monitor raises an alarm (we tested ventricular tachycardia). Trust Layer takes the last 10 seconds of ECG and PPG, gives a score from 0 to 1, and shows one of two verdicts. Red: "Available signals support the monitor alert." Yellow: "Verification inconclusive. The original alert remains active." Yellow does not mean safe: 58 of the 396 yellow alarms in our test were real, so every alarm stays on screen.

HOW IT WORKS. A small LightGBM model (520 KB) on ECG and PPG features. The threshold was set on a separate validation set (495 alarms) and the model was frozen before the test set was read.

RESULT. VTaC test set: 482 ICU alarms, 137 real, 226 patients. Trust Layer marked 86 alarms red and 79 were real: 92% (95% interval 84-98%). Keeping every alarm gives 28%; an ECG-only rule gives 31%. Median 30 ms per alarm, 381 MB peak memory, one laptop thread, no network.

BENEFIT. The crew sees which alarms the signals support without waiting for Earth, and nothing is hidden.

WHY IT IS DIFFERENT. Most work tries to detect events earlier or to suppress false alarms. Trust Layer does neither: it never hides or replaces the monitor's alarm. It adds a second opinion after the alarm, with one plain reason, and marks unconfirmed alarms yellow instead of removing them. It runs fully offline in 30 ms on a laptop, with no cloud and no language model.

WHO BENEFITS. Crews on deep-space missions, where real-time ground support is not available, and hospital ICUs on Earth, where the same alarm-fatigue problem exists. NASA's Exploration Medical Capability work names the lack of real-time ground support as a key driver toward greater autonomy for Moon and Mars missions. Trust Layer is one small autonomy step for crew health monitoring. The Canadian Space Agency's Bio-Monitor smart shirt on the ISS shows that wearable sensors already exist; what is missing for Mars is the on-board check of an alarm.

LIMITS. Earth ICU data, not astronauts. Not clinical, not validated for medical use. Ventricular tachycardia alarms only. The test set was opened twice (an earlier model first, then the final one); the threshold was fixed on validation data first. The continuous event detector is future work.

NEXT. Record real crew data with space labs, build a continuous detector, test how a crew reacts to the verdict.

TOOLS. Python, NumPy, SciPy, pandas, scikit-learn, LightGBM, PyTorch (earlier model), WFDB, NeuroKit2, FastAPI, plain HTML and canvas for the offline demo. Code is on GitHub (link above) with an offline demo in docs/demo.html. https://falafell99.github.io/nasa-trust-layer/cases.html
